source: Original (freshly authored 2026-10-06, calculator allowed); early-finisher extension of 1-10Q_Sequences. u_3 + u_8 = 48, u_12 = 5u_2 give d = 4, u_1 = 6; 124 terms below 500; second sequence 3, 3+d, 3+3d geometric gives d = 3, r = 2. Marks added 2026-10-18 when Chris decided to score the set.

parts.label: a
parts.description: In an arithmetic sequence, u_3 + u_8 = 48 and u_12 = 5u_2. Find the first term u_1 and the common difference d.
parts.tolerance: Accept any valid route, including solving the system 2u_1 + 9d = 48, 4u_1 - 6d = 0 on the GDC.
parts.notes: M1 for u_3 + u_8 = 48 written in terms of u_1 and d, e.g. 2u_1 + 9d = 48. M1 for u_12 = 5u_2 written in terms of u_1 and d, e.g. u_1 + 11d = 5(u_1 + d). A1 for d = 4. A1 for u_1 = 6.
parts.follow_through: Award the final A1 for u_1 correct from the student's own d.

parts.label: b
parts.description: Find the number of terms of this sequence that are less than 500.
parts.tolerance: Accept an equation in place of the inequality, or a table search showing u_124 = 498 and u_125 = 502.
parts.notes: M1 for the nth-term expression set less than (or equal to) 500. A1 for n < 124.5 (or n = 124.5), or the adjacent terms 498 and 502. A1 for the count 124; 124.5 or 125 as the final answer earns A0.
parts.follow_through: Uses u_1 and d from part (a); award marks for work correct from the student's own values.

parts.label: c
parts.description: A different arithmetic sequence has first term 3 and common difference d, d not 0. Its 1st, 2nd and 4th terms are the first three terms of a geometric sequence. Find d and the common ratio of the geometric sequence.
parts.tolerance: Accept the equal-ratio equation in any equivalent form, e.g. (3 + d)^2 = 3(3 + 3d).
parts.notes: (M1) for the terms 3, 3 + d, 3 + 3d, implied by a correct equation. M1 for equating the ratios. A1 for d = 3, with d = 0 rejected or not given; d = 0 offered as a second answer and not rejected earns A0. A1 for r = 2.
parts.follow_through: Award the final A1 for r correct from the student's own d.

source: Original (freshly authored 2026-10-06, calculator allowed); early-finisher extension of 1-7CW_Financial and 1-8CW_Inflation. Sofia 5000 at 4.8% monthly first exceeds 10000 after 15 years; Luca 6000 quarterly to 9000 in 10 years gives r = 4.0752...; Sofia first ahead at the end of year 25.

parts.label: a
parts.description: Sofia invests $5000 at a nominal annual rate of 4.8%, compounded monthly. Find the least number of whole years after which the investment is worth more than $10000.
parts.tolerance: Accept the TVM solver (N = 173.6 months = 14.47 years) as the evidence for the first A1.
parts.notes: M1 for 5000(1 + 4.8/1200)^(12n) compared with 10000, or the TVM entries. A1 for evidence that 14 years is not enough: the 14-year value 9777.63, or N = 14.47 years. A1 for 15 years. A bare 15 with no working earns at most M0A0A1.

parts.label: b
parts.description: Luca invests $6000 at a nominal annual rate of r%, compounded quarterly; after 10 years it is worth $9000. Find r.
parts.tolerance: A1 for 4.08 (3 s.f.) or the calculator display with an ellipsis (4.07527...). 4.075 or 4.0753 with no ellipsis earns A0 with a feedback note to round to 3 s.f.

parts.label: c
parts.description: Find the first whole year at the end of which Sofia's investment is worth more than Luca's.
parts.tolerance: Accept any value consistent with the student's own correctly-rounded r from (b) - including the full-precision r (Luca 15877.07 and 16534.06) and r = 4.08 (Luca 15894.92 and 16553.42). The answer is year 25 either way. Premature rounding of r is a feedback point, not a lost mark.
parts.notes: M1 for both value expressions, or a GDC table of both. A1 for the adjacent-year comparison: Luca ahead at year 24 and Sofia ahead at year 25. A1 for year 25.
parts.follow_through: Uses r from part (b); award marks for a year correct from the student's own r.
